articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Amends Venezuela General License, and Issues Alert
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) today announced new Iran-related designations and updates to existing Iran-related listings. This action aims to further pressure entities involved in activities deemed contrary to U.S. national security and foreign policy interests.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC also published an Iran-related alert to provide guidance and highlight potential risks for businesses and individuals engaging with the region. Additionally, an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ) were issued, signaling adjustments to U.S. policy concerning Venezuela.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's ongoing commitment to utilizing sanctions as a tool to address perceived threats and influence behavior in both Iran and Venezuela.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Iran-related General License. This amendment signifies a modification to existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Iran.

General Licenses are typically issued to authorize categories of transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under sanctions programs. The specifics of this amendment will be crucial for entities engaged in permitted activities with Iran.
The Treasury Department regularly reviews and updates its general licenses to ensure they align with current policy objectives and address evolving circumstances.

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Entities Related to North Korea and Democratic Republic of the Congo
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) announced new designations targeting entities connected to North Korea and the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). These actions aim to disrupt illicit activities and promote U.S. foreign policy objectives in both regions.

The designations against North Korea are part of ongoing efforts to counter its weapons of mass destruction programs and other destabilizing activities. The DRC-related designations likely address issues such as human rights abuses, corruption, or illicit resource extraction.
These measures underscore the U.S. government's commitment to using sanctions to address a range of global threats and promote accountability.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches Settlement Agreement with OFAC
body: Extreme Networks, Inc. has reached a settlement agreement with the U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). This settlement resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions regulations.

Settlement agreements typically involve a monetary penalty and a commitment from the company to implement or enhance compliance measures. Such actions highlight the importance of robust sanctions compliance programs for all U.S. persons and entities.
Details of the alleged violations and the specific terms of the settlement are outlined in the enforcement information published by OFAC.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. These updates provide further clarification and guidance for financial institutions and other entities subject to OFAC regulations.

The FAQs are a critical resource for understanding compliance obligations, particularly concerning the proper handling of blocked or rejected transactions and the timely submission of required reports to OFAC.
Staying abreast of these clarifications is essential for maintaining an effective sanctions compliance program and avoiding potential penalties.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related Entities, Removes Belarus and North Korea Listings, and Issues New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations, alongside the removal of certain entities from the Belarus and North Korea sanctions lists. This multifaceted action reflects evolving U.S. foreign policy considerations.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses and amended existing Frequently Asked Questions. These licenses and FAQs provide crucial guidance on permissible activities under the respective sanctions programs.

The removals from the Belarus and North Korea lists may indicate a recalibration of sanctions strategy or a response to specific developments in those countries, while the new general licenses aim to facilitate certain transactions.

articles.headline: PAIPA Designations Issued by OFAC with Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses.

PAIPA targets individuals and entities involved in the theft of American intellectual property, a critical national security and economic concern. The accompanying General Licenses aim to mitigate unintended consequences of the designations while maintaining the integrity of the sanctions program.
These actions demonstrate the U.S. government's continued efforts to combat intellectual property theft and protect American innovation through the use of sanctions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-Related General License and FAQ
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License and a new Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This update provides further clarity and modifies existing authorizations for certain transactions involving Venezuela.

General Licenses are crucial for navigating the complex landscape of Venezuela sanctions, allowing for specific activities that would otherwise be prohibited. The accompanying FAQ helps clarify the scope and application of the amended license.
These adjustments reflect the ongoing dynamic nature of U.S. sanctions policy towards Venezuela, responding to evolving political and economic conditions.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-Related and Cuba Entities, Issues New and Amended General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation. These actions are coupled with the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

The designations target entities involved in activities that undermine U.S. national security and foreign policy interests in both Iran and Cuba. The new and amended General Licenses aim to provide necessary authorizations for certain humanitarian or other permissible transactions.

These comprehensive measures demonstrate the U.S. government's continued use of sanctions to address perceived threats and influence behavior in these regions, while also providing mechanisms for legitimate activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuela-Related Designation
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced the removal of a Venezuela-related designation. This action indicates a change in the U.S. sanctions posture towards a specific individual or entity previously targeted.

Designation removals can occur for various reasons, including a change in behavior by the designated party, a shift in U.S. foreign policy, or a determination that the designation no longer serves its intended purpose.
This removal signals a potential de-escalation or a targeted adjustment within the broader Venezuela sanctions program.

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Pays $1,529,685 OFAC Civil Penalty

This penalty resolves alleged violations of OFAC sanctions programs. Companies are expected to maintain robust compliance programs to prevent such violations.
The settlement underscores OFAC's continued enforcement efforts to ensure adherence to U.S. sanctions regulations.

The enforcement action highlights the critical importance for financial institutions to implement and maintain comprehensive sanctions compliance programs to prevent illicit transactions.

The case serves as a reminder of the personal liability associated with non-compliance with U.S. sanctions laws.

articles.headline: U.S. Goods and Services Deficit Narrows Slightly in September
body: The U.S. goods and services deficit decreased by $0.7 billion in September, settling at $105.0 billion, a slight improvement from the revised August figure of $105.7 billion.
September exports saw an increase of $5.8 billion, reaching $321.5 billion, while imports also rose by $5.2 billion to $426.6 billion.
Year-to-date, the goods and services deficit has decreased by $92.4 billion, or 12.2 percent, compared to the same period in 2025, with exports increasing by 11.6 percent and imports by 6.2 percent.

articles.headline: Global Central Banks Expected to Continue Rate Hikes Amid Persistent Inflation
body: Analysts anticipate further interest rate increases from central banks globally, including the U.S. Federal Reserve, as inflationary pressures persist, exacerbated by the ongoing conflict in Iran.
The U.S. Federal Reserve maintained its federal funds target range at 3.50%–3.75% in July, but investors expect at least one more rate hike.
The Bank of England is also expected to raise rates, with the European Central Bank likely to follow suit, as higher inflation drives up borrowing costs worldwide.

articles.headline: Oil Prices Fall Below $100 Amid Hopes for Iran Diplomatic Breakthrough
body: Oil prices experienced a significant drop on Wednesday, falling by as much as 9% to trade below $100 a barrel for the first time in a month.
This decline comes as investors react to U.S. midterm election results and express hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough concerning Iran.

Despite the recent fall, Brent crude, the international benchmark, remains significantly higher than its pre-war level of approximately $70, contributing to the International Monetary Fund's (IMF) projection of a 4.7% global headline inflation rate this year.

articles.headline: U.S. and Colombia Launch Joint Military Exercise 'Southern Vanguard 2027'
body: The United States and Colombia have officially launched Exercise Southern Vanguard 2027, a joint military exercise aimed at strengthening readiness and regional security.

The annual exercise, hosted by the Colombian National Army and sponsored by U.S. Southern Command, brings together approximately 800 military personnel to enhance interoperability and bilateral security cooperation.

Building on over 200 years of diplomatic relations, this iteration of Southern Vanguard, scheduled to run until mid-November, seeks to improve soldiers' skills and their ability to operate effectively in challenging environments across the Western Hemisphere.

articles.headline: Zelenskyy Confirms 40 Dead in 'Insane' Russian School Attack Ahead of Peace Talks
body: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has confirmed that 40 people are now dead and over 30 missing following a devastating Russian attack on a school in Ukraine on Monday.
The attack, which hit power stations in Kyiv and Zhytomyr and a cargo vessel near Odesa, occurred just days before crucial trilateral peace talks involving the U.S. and Russia.
Zelenskyy's comments came as he continued his European tour, visiting Germany and expected in Spain, while the EU hosted technical talks with the U.S., NATO, and the World Bank on Ukraine.

articles.headline: French Blood Banks Hit by Cyber-Attack, Alarm Systems Prevent Compromise
body: French blood banks have been targeted in the latest cyber-attack to hit Europe, with the French blood service (EFS) reporting that temperature and defrosting thresholds were raised to "very high levels" during the incident.
Fortunately, the EFS stated that its alarm systems allowed technicians to intervene before any blood products were compromised.

The EFS, France's public blood transfusion operator, plays a vital role in collecting, testing, preparing, and distributing blood products to over 1,900 hospitals, supporting more than a million patients annually.

articles.headline: OCC Announces October 2026 Enforcement Actions, Including $750 Million Penalty Against Bank of America
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) released its enforcement actions for October 2026, which included a significant $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, National Association.

This penalty was imposed due to deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and issues with sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information.

Additionally, the OCC issued a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and identification program violations.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: FinCEN Assesses $1.2 Billion Penalty Against Bank of America for BSA/AML Failures
body: The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network (FinCEN) has assessed a staggering $1.2 billion civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. for willful violations of the Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and its implementing regulations.

The penalty stems from the bank's failure to implement and maintain an adequate anti-money laundering (AML) program, conduct due diligence on foreign financial institution correspondent accounts, and file suspicious activity reports for over $5 billion in transactions.

FinCEN credited a $750 million penalty concurrently assessed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) against its total, meaning Bank of America will pay $450 million directly to FinCEN.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers to EAR
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.
This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms, reducing compliance burdens on the firearms industry while maintaining national security.

Under this new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, with license exceptions similar to those available for firearms also applicable.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
